"Folie à deux" is a French phrase. "Folie" means madness or lunacy. "À" means of or for. "Deux" means two. So the phrase translates literally to "madness of two" — a shared madness between two people.
The Core Idea in One Sentence

Folie à deux is a rare psychiatric phenomenon where one person's delusion is "transmitted" to another person through close, prolonged contact, causing both of them to share the same false belief.

That's the heart of it. One person genuinely goes mad with a specific delusion. A second person, who was previously mentally healthy, begins to believe the same delusion — not because they independently went mad, but because they absorbed it from the first person through the sheer force of closeness and emotional influence.
What is a Delusion?

Before going further, it helps to be precise about the word "delusion," because it's used loosely in everyday life but has a strict meaning in psychiatry.

A delusion is a fixed, false belief that a person holds with absolute certainty, that is clearly contradicted by reality, and that cannot be changed by presenting them with evidence or logical arguments.

Examples:

  • "The government has implanted a chip in my brain to monitor my thoughts."
  • "My neighbors are slowly poisoning me through my food."
  • "My family has been replaced by identical-looking imposters."

These aren't metaphors or exaggerations. The person who holds a delusion genuinely, unshakeably believes it to be true. That is the kind of belief involved in folie à deux.
A Brief History: Where the Term Came From

The term was formally introduced in 1877 by two French psychiatrists named Charles Lasègue and Jean-Pierre Falret. They published a paper describing cases where two people in close emotional proximity came to share an identical delusional system.

Before their work, these cases were described in isolated observations but had no unifying label. Lasègue and Falret systematized the pattern, described the social dynamics involved, and gave the psychiatric world a framework for thinking about it.

The phenomenon has had several official clinical names over the decades:

  • Folie à deux (the original French term, still widely used)
  • Shared psychotic disorder (used in the DSM-IV, the American diagnostic manual from 1994)
  • Induced delusional disorder (used in the ICD-10, the World Health Organization's diagnostic system)

In the most recent American psychiatric manual, DSM-5 (2013), shared psychotic disorder was removed as a standalone diagnosis, with the reasoning that it could be captured under other existing categories. However, the concept itself remains clinically and academically relevant, and the term folie à deux is still very much in active use.
The Two People Involved: Primary and Secondary

In virtually every case, there are two distinct roles.

The Primary Person (the "Inducer")

This is the person who develops the delusion first and independently. They have a genuine psychotic illness — most commonly paranoid schizophrenia or a delusional disorder. Their delusion is intense, elaborate, and unshakeable. They are typically the more dominant personality in the relationship: more forceful, more emotionally controlling, or more persuasive.

The Secondary Person (the "Recipient")

This is the person who adopts the delusion from the primary person. Crucially, before the relationship with the primary person, they were usually mentally healthy. They are often more passive, more dependent, and more suggestible. They are not "mad" on their own; their shared belief is a product of the relationship.

The secondary person genuinely comes to believe the delusion. It's not performance, loyalty, or pretending to keep the peace. Over time, through constant reinforcement and emotional pressure, the delusion becomes real in their mind.
How Does It Happen? The Mechanics

For folie à deux to develop, several conditions typically come together:

1. Prolonged closeness and isolation
The two people live or spend time together intensely, often cut off from the wider world. This isolation is key — it means the outside reality never effectively challenges or corrects the delusional worldview. The primary person's version of reality fills all the available space.

2. A strong emotional bond with a power imbalance
The relationship is usually one of deep emotional dependence. Common pairings include married couples, parent and child, two siblings, or close friends. Crucially, the secondary person looks up to, loves, fears, or relies on the primary person heavily. This creates a psychological vulnerability to adopting the primary's beliefs.

3. The primary person is persuasive and insistent
The primary person's delusional framework is not quiet — it shapes every interaction. They interpret daily events through its lens. Over months or years, through sheer repetition and emotional weight, this worldview seeps into the secondary person's beliefs.

4. A lack of corrective outside contact
If the secondary person had frequent, warm, trusted social connections outside the pair, those external relationships might provide reality-checking. In folie à deux cases, this corrective network is typically absent or has been deliberately severed.
The Most Important Test: What Happens When They're Separated?

This is one of the most clinically fascinating aspects of the phenomenon. In many cases, when the two people are separated, the secondary person's delusion fades on its own.

This is what distinguishes the secondary person from someone with an independent psychotic illness. Their belief was not rooted in their own biology or individual mental breakdown — it was propped up by the relationship. Remove the relationship, remove the constant reinforcement, reconnect them with reality, and the delusion can dissolve within weeks or months without any medication.

The primary person, by contrast, does not recover simply from separation. Their delusion has its own internal roots and requires active psychiatric treatment.
Types: The Different Varieties Psychiatrists Described

Over the years, clinicians refined the original concept into subtypes based on what exactly happens between the two people.

Folie imposée ("imposed madness")
The most common type. The secondary person passively absorbs the delusion. They were mentally healthy before, they adopt the belief through the relationship, and if separated early enough, they recover well. The delusion is "imposed" on them from outside.

Folie communiquée ("communicated madness")
The secondary person initially resists the delusion — they don't just passively receive it. But over a longer period, the primary person's reality eventually "wins." What makes this type particularly interesting is that even after separation, the secondary person may hold onto the delusion. By the time it's "communicated" fully, it has taken genuine root.

Folie simultanée ("simultaneous madness")
Both people independently develop the same or similar delusions at roughly the same time. Unlike the other types, there is no clear direction of transmission. Both people are primary in a sense. This is relatively rare and controversial as a subtype, since it raises the question of whether they truly influenced each other or simply had similar vulnerabilities and experiences.

Folie induite ("induced madness")
This occurs when someone who already has a psychotic illness adopts additional delusions from someone they're living with who also has a psychotic illness. It's less about transmitting madness to a healthy person and more about one set of delusional ideas cross-pollinating with another.
Extensions Beyond Two People

The concept was never strictly limited to pairs. The same dynamic can involve more people:

  • Folie à trois — madness of three
  • Folie à quatre — madness of four
  • Folie à famille — madness of a family
  • Folie à plusieurs — madness of several (a group or crowd)

In all these cases, the same basic mechanics apply: a charismatic or dominant primary individual with a delusional belief system, close and isolated contact, and a group whose members come to share that belief.

This extension is why the concept is relevant to understanding cults. A charismatic cult leader with delusional or paranoid beliefs can, through isolation, emotional manipulation, and constant reinforcement, cause an entire community to sincerely adopt those beliefs. The Heaven's Gate group and the Jonestown massacre are historical examples that scholars have analyzed through this lens.
Who Is at Risk of Becoming the Secondary Person?

Not everyone in close contact with someone delusional will develop folie à deux. Several factors seem to raise the risk:

  • Emotional dependence: The more you need this person — for love, security, identity — the more vulnerable you are to their reality.
  • Social isolation: The fewer outside connections and reality-checks you have, the more your entire sense of what's real can be shaped by one person.
  • Pre-existing passivity or lower self-assertiveness: People who are naturally more passive or who defer to others are more susceptible.
  • Lower premorbid intelligence or education has been cited in some older literature, though this is debated and should be understood in context.
  • Shared stress or trauma: When two people are going through intense experiences together, the bonds deepen and the vulnerability increases.

It is important to note that none of this makes the secondary person weak or foolish. The conditions of folie à deux are extreme — prolonged isolation, intense emotional dependency, daily reinforcement of a distorted reality. Most human minds, under those conditions, can be shaped in ways they otherwise wouldn't be.
Real-World Examples

June and Jennifer Gibbons — "The Silent Twins"

Perhaps the most widely studied human example. These identical twin sisters from Wales became famous for refusing to speak to anyone except each other. They lived in a world almost entirely of their own making. Their case is complex — they had distinct shared beliefs, rituals, and perceptions of reality that were not accessible to or shared by anyone outside their bond. While not a textbook delusional case in the strictest clinical sense, their extreme mutual psychological enmeshment is one of the most cited examples of the folie à deux dynamic in the broader sense.

Ian Brady and Myra Hindley — The Moors Murderers

Brady was the dominant, psychopathic primary figure. Hindley, before meeting him, had no history of violence or criminal behavior. After years under his intense influence and isolation from outside relationships, she participated in the murders of five children in 1960s England. Many analysts have used the folie à deux framework to understand how a person with no independent violent pathology could be so thoroughly absorbed into another person's psychopathology.

Cult leaders and their followers

Jim Jones (Jonestown, 1978) and Marshall Applewhite of Heaven's Gate are studied as examples where the dynamic scaled up. The leader held a coherent, elaborate delusional framework. Through isolation, love-bombing, sleep deprivation, dietary control, and constant ideological reinforcement, entire communities came to share beliefs that — from outside — were clearly disconnected from reality. Over 900 people died at Jonestown. 39 members of Heaven's Gate died by mass suicide believing they would board a spacecraft hidden in the tail of the Hale-Bopp comet.
How Is It Diagnosed?

Diagnosis requires careful clinical assessment. The psychiatrist or psychologist evaluating the case needs to:

  • Establish that both people share an identical or near-identical delusional belief system
  • Confirm that the secondary person did not independently develop the delusion
  • Understand the nature and history of the relationship (closeness, isolation, power dynamics)
  • Rule out independent psychotic disorders in the secondary person
  • Rule out organic causes (brain tumors, substance use, medical conditions that can mimic psychosis)

Diagnosis is complicated by the fact that both people will typically deny there is anything wrong. From inside the shared delusion, everything makes perfect sense.
How Is It Treated?

Treatment generally involves three components:

1. Separation
The single most important intervention, especially for the secondary person. Physical separation from the primary person removes the constant reinforcement and gives the secondary person a chance to reconnect with outside reality. In many cases, especially early ones, this alone leads to significant recovery in the secondary person.

2. Treating the Primary Person
The primary person's underlying psychiatric condition — typically schizophrenia, delusional disorder, or a mood disorder with psychotic features — must be treated with antipsychotic medication, therapy, and psychiatric care. Without treating the root, even if separated, re-exposure risks the cycle starting again.

3. Psychotherapy for the Secondary Person
Even if the delusion fades after separation, the secondary person may need therapy to process what happened. They often struggle with confusion about what was real, shame, grief over the relationship, and the challenge of rebuilding a sense of themselves and their reality.

Prognosis is generally better for the secondary person than for the primary person. The secondary person's condition is, in many cases, fundamentally relational rather than biological — which means addressing the relationship can directly address the illness.
In Popular Culture

The term and concept have entered popular culture in several ways:

  • The 2024 film "Joker: Folie à Deux" used the term in its title, exploring the shared delusion or co-dependent reality between Arthur Fleck (the Joker) and his love interest.
  • The phrase is used loosely in many crime dramas, thrillers, and discussions of toxic relationships to describe any situation where two people reinforce each other's distorted thinking — though it's worth knowing this popular use is sometimes broader and less precise than the clinical definition.
  • It appears frequently in discussions of codependency, cults, radicalization, and echo chambers, as a conceptual lens even when not a strict clinical diagnosis.
The Broader Lesson

Beyond its clinical definition, folie à deux points to something profound about human psychology: reality is, to a significant degree, socially constructed. Our sense of what is true, normal, and real is constantly shaped by the people around us. Most of the time, living in society with many different relationships provides enough corrective feedback to keep us grounded.

But when we are isolated, dependent on one person, and that person holds a distorted version of reality — our minds are far more malleable than we might assume. This is not a sign of stupidity or weakness. It is a feature of how human cognition works. We are deeply social animals, and our sense of reality is deeply social too.

This is why isolation is a weapon — in abusive relationships, in cults, in authoritarian systems. Remove someone from the corrective network of a diverse social world, and the reality offered by whoever remains is the reality that fills the mind.
Summary at a Glance

• What: A shared delusional disorder where one person's delusion is transmitted to another through close contact.
  • Who: A dominant primary person with psychosis, and a dependent secondary person who absorbs the belief.
  • How: Through isolation, emotional dependency, and constant reinforcement over time.
  • Key test: Separate them — the secondary person's delusion often fades; the primary person's does not.
  • Types: Folie imposée, communiquée, simultanée, and induite.
  • Scale: Can extend to three people, families, or entire groups.
  • Treatment: Separation, treating the primary's psychosis, and therapy for the secondary.
  • Deeper meaning: A window into how malleable human reality can be under extreme social influence.
